claim.why_it_matters: In an index the leading indent is the ONLY thing that marks a sub-entry as belonging to its parent. Flattening it detaches sub-items from their parents and promotes them to look like top-level index terms. The transcription is also self-inconsistent: pages 1237, 1238, 1239 and 1243 DO preserve the level with   runs, while pages 1235, 1236, 1240, 1241, 1242, 1244, 1245, 1246 (and the right-hand 'Category of data' block on 1237, md lines 64-79) drop it entirely. The worst reading arises on page 1244, where the sub-entry 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph 312' (under FILE STATUS clause) is flattened and lands immediately above the genuine top-level entry 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph 311', so the two read as a contradictory duplicate. Index only - no normative text is affected.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED on both sides, but the claim understates the scope and mislabels the kind.

PDF side (rendered at 300 dpi, then re-cropped and upscaled 2x over the DYNAMIC block to read the glyph origins directly): the printed page sets 'DYNAMIC 430', 'Dynamic access mode 221, 1009', 'DYNAMIC LENGTH clause 397', 'DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause 291' and 'DYNAMIC phrase' all on one common left margin, and sets 'Data description entry 363' at a visibly deeper margin (roughly one em-and-a-half further right). The indent is unmistakable at that magnification and is not an OCR or rasterization artifact. The claim quotes the PDF accurately.

Markdown side: specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 50830-50832 read exactly 'DYNAMIC LENGTH clause [397](#page-397)' / 'Data description entry [363](#page-363)' / 'DYNAMIC LENGTH STRUCTURE clause [291](#page-291)', all three flush left with no leading whitespace and no   run. The claim quotes the markdown accurately.

Why this is NOT dismissible as mere formatting: the transcription itself treats index level as content and encodes it with a four-fold ' ' run. Page 1237 (lines 50351-50382) does exactly that - '    Continuation of [37]', '    CLASS clause [382]', and so on - and the same convention appears throughout the later index (e.g. lines 52458, 52683, 52733, 52802). Page 1240 drops it for every sub-entry. So this is a defect measured against the document's own established representation scheme, not a stylistic choice by the transcriber, and it yields readings that are simply wrong: 'Data description entry 363' is promoted to a top-level index term, where it also collides with the genuine sub-entry of the same wording at line 50831's page-top counterpart (line 6 of the page).

The claim's supporting rationale about page 1244 also checks out independently: lines 51287-51288 are 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph [312](#page-312)' immediately followed by 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph [311](#page-311)', both flush left, which does read as a contradictory duplicate.

Two inaccuracies in the claim, neither fatal: (1) the kind 'misplaced-content' is wrong - no content is misplaced, reordered, or moved between lines; every line is present, in the right sequence, attached to the right page. What is lost is the structural indentation encoding index nesting level. (2) The claim scopes the defect to a single three-line block. In fact essentially every sub-entry on page 1240 is flattened - about 47 lines across both columns (left column: the page-top 'Data description entry 363' plus Definition/Identifier/Qualified/Scope of/Subscripted, Definition 510, INITIALIZE 637, three ACCEPT 576 lines, TYPE clause 494, the 60559 reference, Definition 301, FLOAT-DECIMAL 275, USAGE 504, Definition 301, SPECIAL-NAMES 290, USE 774, Normal completion 548, INITIALIZE 637, SET locale 731; right column: STRING 759 through Definition 158). The DYNAMIC LENGTH trio is one instance of a page-wide loss, not the defect itself.

One nearby difference correctly NOT counted: 'DEFAULT ROUNDED MODE IS PROHIBITED clause 563, 1195' is printed over two lines in the PDF with '1195' on an indented continuation; the markdown joins it into one line (line 59). That is benign line-wrap furniture, not a lost level.

Severity 'cosmetic' is right - this is the alphabetic index, entirely non-normative, and no rule, format diagram, or general rule is affected.
verdict.corrected_description: Lost index nesting level (structural indentation), page-wide - not misplaced content. On page 1240 the transcription drops the leading indent from every sub-entry, roughly 47 lines across both columns, promoting each to look like a top-level index term. The cited instance is real: the PDF prints 'Data description entry  363' indented one level beneath 'DYNAMIC LENGTH clause  397' (verified by 2x crop of the 300 dpi render - the sub-entry's glyph origin sits about one and a half ems right of the surrounding top-level entries), while specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 50830-50832 set all three flush left. Text, ordering and page assignment are fully correct; only the level markup is missing. This is a defect against the transcription's own convention, which encodes index level with '    ' runs on pages 1237-1239 and 1243 and elsewhere in the index. The claim's page-1244 corroboration is accurate (md lines 51287-51288 place a flattened 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph [312]' directly above the genuine top-level 'FILE-CONTROL paragraph [311]'). Index only; no normative text affected; cosmetic. Fix is mechanical: re-apply the four-fold   prefix to sub-entries on the affected index pages.
